claims.claim: A persona is a fictional, yet realistic, description of a typical or target user of the product (NN/g working definition); it is a composite portrait that puts a single face to many users, and the IxDF calls personas model characters or composite characters composed from data collected from many individuals.

A useful persona includes demographics (age, gender, occupation), behaviors, needs/concerns/goals, experience level, and context (how and how often the person would use the product); every detail must be able to affect a design decision or it should be removed.

The core rule of persona creation is that personas are research-based: they might be made-up people, but they should be based on information about real people gathered through methods such as interviews, surveys, field studies, and longitudinal studies; inventing a persona from imagination produces a stereotype with a name.

Well-executed personas require qualitative research with real users to uncover the why behind behavior, and good personas go beyond demographics: demographic facts suit marketing decisions, while design decisions need behavioral and attitudinal detail.

Personas exist to keep the team focused on a concrete user: they build empathy, help the team resist the temptation to design for everyone, and create a common, precise vocabulary in which the persona's name acts as shorthand for a full set of attributes, desires, and behaviors.

A persona differs from a stereotype: a persona is a research-based, fictional character representing a user type and is revised when evidence arrives, while a stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified, generalized belief about a group that is often held without evidence and leads to bias.

Personas represent types, not individuals: no real user is exactly a persona, personas should not be treated as an exhaustive taxonomy of every possible user type, and a persona is a thinking tool that never replaces testing a real product with real users.

Personas are snapshots in time: as the business, the technology, or the user base changes, personas drift out of date, so they must be revised when the business or technology changes significantly or when new research shows the user base has shifted.

Teams keep the persona set small because personas must stay memorable, actionable, and distinct from one another, and more personas mean less focus; in practice most teams settle on three to five personas with one primary persona anchoring the design and secondary personas covering important variations.

Personas and jobs-to-be-done are compatible tools that answer different questions: a persona describes who the user is (goals, behaviors, frustrations), while a jobs-to-be-done describes what job the user is hiring the product to do.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are personas and archetypes the same thing, and is one preferable? Some teams use the terms interchangeably, and jobs-to-be-done framing is sometimes positioned as an alternative to personas.
positions: Personas and archetypes both summarize the same research clusters of user types.
NN/g distinguishes them by presentation: a persona presents the type as a single named human character, while an archetype uses an abstract label without a name or face.
Jobs-to-be-done is sometimes presented as a replacement for personas rather than a complement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The tools answer different questions and are complementary: personas describe who the user is, archetypes summarize the same clusters without a named character, and jobs-to-be-done describe what job the product is hired for. NN/g treats personas and archetypes as compatible, and personas-plus-jobs-to-be-done is a common combined practice, so the lesson presents all three as complementary rather than competing.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's framing of personas as 'a foundational concept' students 'use to organize information' — generic boilerplate with no method content.

The draft's implication that personas can be written up directly from team knowledge ('we know our users, just write one up') — contradicts the research-based core rule and is explicitly corrected in Common Mistakes.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic boilerplate draft with a sourced working definition of personas (Nielsen Norman Group), the composite-portrait framing, the persona anatomy (demographics, goals, frustrations, behaviors, context), and the research-based core rule.
Added the honest limits: personas represent types not individuals, are snapshots in time requiring revision, and never replace testing with real users.
All examples rewritten as original, invented scenarios (Market Mornings farmers-market app; personas Owen, Dev, and Marta) per subject guidance that examples must be original.
